utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. And good morning to you. The usual advisory, if there are any problems with interpretation, please let me know. I see no significant absences amongst the Defence teams. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Nicholls. I think we can start. Good morning to you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope you had a good weekend.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will make every effort to try and bring your testimony to the end -- to an end the earliest possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't seem that convinced.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We will see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So who is next? You're going to follow the same order as before, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, we are with this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek is defending, together with Mr. Ostojic, Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. How are you?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did you have a nice weekend?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You shouldn't repeat questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It's such a good question, Your Honour. Could I have a little help on the ELMO? This is -- for identification purposes I will not give it a number. For the record, this is a copy of the hand -- the notes that this witness has been referring to throughout his direct testimony and I'd ask that page 1 be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Colonel Beara -- Colonel Boering, excuse me, I have placed on the ELMO a copy which I believe to be your handwritten notes; is that a fact?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And this is the very first page of those notes, correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And were these notes generated on the 14th of September 2006?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some of them were. Others, when I was busy preparing in the waiting room and was alone, I would just jot down some names to speed things up; so some were, some weren't. It varies. They are just some notes. They don't appear in any logical sequence. You requested a copy. You're welcome to have one but I used this to make faster headway. It's not a heavy document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, I see 14 September in upper left-hand middle. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So is that the day this first page of notes was generated by you, if you remember, sir?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's perfectly conceivable but the page I have in front of me for today's starts with 25 September and it reads, "the second defender, Mr. Meek."

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm not concerned with your notes for today's testimony but trust me, I will be. I want to know about the ones on the ELMO. Can you see them on the right screen?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: These notes were taken during your proofing session with Mr. McCloskey of the OTP, were they not?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's partly correct but partly incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Why don't we move right down to number 6 and I'm not sure 6 is on the ELMO. I only see 1 through 4. There we go. Number 6 appears to be your handwriting and it says, Beara, correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Then next to that I think is your handwritten in English, meeting, is that what it says, underlined twice?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And then to the right, it looks like March April with a line under March and above April, that being circled; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: March, April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And then underneath -- and that's circled, correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Underneath that you have May/June; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And right to the right of that you have McCloskey underlined, correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You can't read your own handwriting, sir?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I really can't read it at this time. I'll take a look at the original, if you really want to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't even read it myself at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You'll agree with me it appears to be a capital M and a little C and then C-l-l-s-k-y [as spelt]?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I really don't discern that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Why was May -- the May/June circled, if you can tell me, sir? March/April, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was a meeting in late March or early April. It's a messy way of jotting it down quickly. I assume that I must have done that during one of the breaks in the room where I was waiting. Occasionally I would prepare something and think back about exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: On the far right, you have -- and looks like a parentheses perhaps. Can you read your handwriting on that note?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, does it say military personnel?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It's in English, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't figure it out at this time. I'm not playing games with you but I wrote it down very quickly. Perhaps it was to organise my own thoughts. I just don't remember any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. Did you have your proofing session on 14 September with Peter McCloskey from the Office of the Prosecutor, Colonel Boering?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact dates any more but about two weeks ago, it was on a Thursday, and Friday, I believe, I was here. So if I think back, I could calculate whether that was the 14th. It's perfectly conceivable.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm not so concerned about the actual date but was it Peter McCloskey you did your proofing session with the first day?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't with him, no. He greeted me very briefly and subsequently I was handed over to somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: When you greeted him, Peter McCloskey, very briefly or when you were handed over to somebody else were you told that McCloskey wanted you to mention Ljubisa Beara [Realtime transcript read in error "maurz"] in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't come in -- it didn't come into the picture. He greeted me would briefly told me he was happy I was there and subsequently I was handed over to somebody else. I don't remember anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, if the usher could just move it over to the next page under number 9. Colonel, I'll just ask you can you read your own handwriting under number 9?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: One moment, because this is important. In line 22 on the previous page, page 5, Mr. Meek's question should read, "You mention Beara," not "maurz," "in your testimony." Beara, because "maurz" doesn't mean anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a significant alteration that needs to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, and I appreciate you pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Let's go back to 9 that you are circled on the second page of your handwritten notes you've been referring to in your direct examination, please.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And now -- and very quickly, that sheet notes it was the 15th of September, correct? I think that's going to be further down, Colonel Boering.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: On my original copy I don't see anything about September 15. I don't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You're correct. You're correct. That's about the fourth page. I'm going to skip that for right now. Can you read your own handwriting on 9, that is circled?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see, "Three meetings in Fontana there, 11 and 12. 11/12" and after that it reads, "Read through."

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I ask you a question, Colonel? These are notes prepared by you for yourself for the purpose of this testimony to speed up. Why did you prepare them in English and not in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sometimes I write in English, sometimes I write in Dutch. In Ministry I work with a Dutch general and sometimes I speak English with him too. It intermingles. Sometimes we speak English, sometimes we speak Dutch. We are a bit sloppy about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, just turn to the very last page of your notes before, I mean the notes that we made copies of last week, if you would. And I'll tell you right now it says 15 September, S-e-p-t, 0900 Julian. You see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have it on the ELMO, Madam Usher, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Colonel Boering, I take it you met with Julian from the Office of the Prosecutor on the 15th of September for further proofing for your direct testimony, correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's perfectly possible. I assume that to have been the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to ask you to just look to your right to the lawyer sitting right there who questioned you on direct examination, do you have any personal recollection of meeting with him on the 15th of September or any time prior to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Why would you tell me that it's entirely possible, then?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that gets back to the 14th and the 15th. I have to check my diary, if you want to know exactly, and look at Thursday and Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We may look at that in a moment. Now, going back to the first page, if you just skim that for a moment, Colonel Boering, I submit to you that this is exactly the outline of your direct examination, was it not?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see several -- there is a certain pattern here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And that pattern was suggested to you by the Office of the Prosecutor, the people you met with, to proof you and get you prepared for your testimony here in this Court, correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these subjects would be addressed in this fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Please tell me which member of the Office of the Prosecutor staff told you, you needed to testify about Colonel Beara when you testified?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir. I think that's all we need for the ELMO, right now. Colonel Boering, on your direct examination you talked a little bit about the structure of DutchBat III; do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you please just give me an overview of what the structure of DutchBat III was, starting with who was the chief, the top commander?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can I intervene for a moment? Does a document exist which shows the entire structure? That could help us get through this. Because if it does it may simplify matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe it does. He talked about the -- Karremans and Franken. I just want to go through it briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But in the meantime if we can follow better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll check, Your Honour. I don't have one right at my fingertips. I'm not sure whether we have such a diagram at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Go ahead. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Colonel Boering, was Lieutenant Colonel Karremans the head guy there, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: But of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did he have a deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He had one locally, that was Major Franken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And just -- Colonel, just going on down the line, just tell us who was underneath Franken, then.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, please do.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: What would you like to know about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I would just like to know their names and who they were over.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was somebody who was major of operations; that was Major Frahagen [phoen]. There was somebody who was responsible for II; that was Captain Weaver [phoen]. There was somebody for personnel; that was Captain Foreman. And there was the camp base commander; that was Captain Hrun [phoen]. He was in Srebrenica. And there was a camp base commander for Potocari; that it was Captain Matajson [phoen]. And there was a commander for staff care; that was Major van Beeren [phoen]. Those were a few names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You were the liaison officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: S5-liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your direct superior would have been who, sir?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was Lieutenant Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So when you reported, you reported directly to Karremans and not through his deputy commander, Franken, is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes the communication went through Major Franken. Sometimes it was via Karremans. It depended how busy Karremans was and the reporting procedure. Major Franken was also led of logistics. In the first part of my work, which related to requests from the Muslim population for care, hospitals, schools and the like, we would examine first whether we could handle the logistics, and then Major Franken would be assigned to that. So before I reported things to I -- to Lieutenant Colonel Frankens [as interpreted], I would first check with Major Franken whether we would be able to arrange that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would you have daily meetings, sir, during this period, from January of 1995 until July 1995? And when I say that, I mean daily meetings with your DutchBat people.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the morning would start around half past 7.00, with the staff getting together, and in the afternoon, I believe around 3.00 or half past 3.00 a small group of the staff would review the events of the day, often including Lieutenant Colonel Karremans, Major Franken, and myself, and perhaps two or three others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did you and/or others generate written reports, say, after your 3.00 or 3.30 p.m. meetings on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reported to my superiors in Tuzla once a week. There were internal reports among the five of us orally, or writing down in a tiny little booklet about what happened. The battalion drafted a daily situation report to the superiors and sometimes there was a paragraph about CIMIC and the liaison, and I would then be asked to write that out or check whether it was accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Who was the officer or individual who had the job to keep custody of the tiny little booklet where you wrote down things that happened on a daily basis, sir?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have an individual who was responsible for storing things and writing them down for me. There was somebody who often accompanied me. That was Sergeant-Major Rave, and he would also jot down somethings for his own work so at meetings, when we were together, I often was the spokesperson and he would take notes, and after the meeting we would review them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You didn't destroy those, did you? Didn't you keep that tiny little book?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned to Kladanj, I didn't have a lot with me. I had a T-shirt, some shorts, and a pistol, not my things. My things were sent back to me later on, and some things were missing. At any rate, I don't have any more notes from that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: If you know, Colonel Boering, what happened to all of the daily sit-coms that were sent to Tuzla and elsewhere from DutchBat III?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Boering, you discussed in your direct examination two meetings with Mr. Beara, did you not? Do you recall that today? I know it was last week but do you recall that today?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember, and it's also in the notes of mine that you quoted from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And last week, you testified that your memory was much better in 1995 than it is today; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are talking about the things that happened at the time, there are many things that I could remember far back then than I do now. I remember perfectly well what happened yesterday at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you recall testifying under oath last week that memories do fade and that you had a better recollection of what occurred in 1995 from January through July 12th, than you did last week, for example?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if this question is formulated correctly but as I read it back here, it sounds very illogical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Let me rephrase it. Do you believe that your memory concerning the events that the Office of the Prosecutor has brought you here to testify about are better today than they were in 1995, soon after the events occurred and when they were fresh on your memory?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, this is taking too long and I suggest instead of going in a round about fashion, if you have a source that you would like to confront the witness with, go straight there. Do exactly like Mr. Nicholls did when he was examining the witness in chief, and then put the question to him whether he believes that his recollection, previous recollection, nearer to the date is more reliable. Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just for the record I think at page 12, line 9, the witness agreed to the proposition in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes but he also contested the way the question was being put so he did agree, I agree with you, but if there is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's fine, judge. I thought he agreed too and I didn't -- so I'll go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead because we are going around in circles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness Exhibit 2 D00004 [sic]. By the way, for the record, while the witness is looking at this, this is his witness statement 28 September 1995, given to the Office of the Prosecutor. Interviewer was Erma Oosterman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, as a preliminary matter, Colonel Boering, you reviewed all of your written statements before you came here to testify, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was given all of them to read over but I didn't read all of them over, considering how thick the document was. I had to leaf through quite a bit quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, Exhibit 2 D0004 is only eight pages long, nine pages long. Did you read it? It's your very first statement to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I read it. I scanned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Will you please -- I could be happy to give you a hard copy so that we don't have to go page through page. Can you point out where in your first statement to the OTP, September 28, 1995, approximately three and a half months after the events were fresh on your mind, where Mr. Beara is mentioned by you even one time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I think the witness needs to have a copy of this statement at his disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I have completely clean copies if you need it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to have a look at the copy that Mr. Meek has --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I remember this first examination correctly, I believe it was by Mrs. Oosterman. The main focus was rapes and abuse of women. That's what the examination was focused on so it wasn't an in-depth examination but focused on wrong doings that I saw. That's what's in my memory. Perhaps I should read it to dredge it back in my memory but the examination always reflects the purpose of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: ? Very well, Colonel. Let's just look at that for a minute, then. Page 2 of the statement, Witness statement, which is really page 1, where you start, just skim down through it. You talk about the people you made contact with and maintained contact with on both sides of this action, the Muslim army and the Serbian army, correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You talk about Suvanovic [phoen], Nikolic, Sarkic, Vukovic, correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it reads.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm already on the second page. Haven't seen anything about rapes. Do you?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this being the purpose of the investigation. Perhaps I heard that in the introduction to the conversation. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Perhaps you're thinking about a different statement, correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. Let's just go on down the next page. Then you start talking about the contacts you had with the Muslim soldiers, correct? Naser Oric, Ramic, Ekrem, Zulfo, you see that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Then you talk a little bit about the mayor of Srebrenica and the deputy mayor, correct? I'm looking at page 4.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now I'm looking at page 5, now you go into the meetings at the Hotel Fontana, correct? Even on page 6 you're still talking about the meetings, correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Page 7, still on the meetings, aren't we, and your drive back to Bratunac and the voluntary evacuation, correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Page 8 and the end of your statement is 9, talks about you leaving with the column and where you're dropped off in the vicinity of Kladanj. You see that, the last page?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. Well, appears to me that Erma Oosterman was asking you a lot about the different personalities and soldiers from the ABiH army and the Bosnian Serb army, wasn't she?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see what I said at the time, and what the questions were. I can see, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you'll agree with me that your memory of the events and the personalities and the players during that time period were much fresher on your memory in September of 1995 than they were in 1998 or 2000 when you testified in Krstic, or even last week, isn't that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In 1995, it's fresher in your memory than in 1998 or 2000. Perhaps they probed a bit more at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And again, just for the record, you never one time mentioned Mr. Beara in your first debriefing to the OTP, September 28, 1995, did you, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see it in this text, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you gave several different debriefings and statements to the Dutch military and government, did you not?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did you deem it appropriate to review those before you came here to testify?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I came here, I asked the Prosecutor to refresh my memory, and I was able to review some things here, and looked at the NIOD report as well, to the best of my ability. NIOD being the Netherlands State Institute of War Documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel, for that answer. Nowhere in any of your debriefings to the Dutch government, did you ever mention Mr. Beara, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to take up any more time with this issue but I tell you what, Colonel. I will give you copies of each one of those statements I have. You can read them at the break and, if I'm wrong, you can tell me. Would that be fair?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. I would object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we didn't give you permission to speak, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Colonel, what's your position on the proposition that has been made to you by Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wonder whether he has all the statements I made to the Ministry of Defence or the Dutch government. But if he's willing to give them to me, I'll be happy to look and see whether they are complete but I don't know whether they are complete because I made so many statements, including some in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Does that answer your question, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, it does, Your Honour. I'll be happy to give him everything I have from the Dutch government, his statements which I have received from the Office of the Prosecutor. I honestly don't know if I have everything. We always wonder whether we have all the statements in this business. I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Colonel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And how long would the break need to be, then?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Oh, the same amount of time, Judge. They are short statements. They are only a page or two long, the ones I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And then he will tell us whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Not now. We don't need a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course not. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Boering, can you tell us, please, when was the first time that you remember that you ever mentioned Mr. Beara in any of your statements?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls? What was your objection to the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: None. I was just thinking instead of giving the witness homework during the break he could just put the statements in and then the Trial Chamber could see for themselves whether it's mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we still need to know when that is a complete picture of his statements to the Dutch authorities or not. At the end of the day, yes, we can read them or -- but that's not the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Colonel Boering, can I put it to you that the first time that you ever mention my client, Mr. Beara, was when you asked the Prosecutor to refresh your memory? You just said that under oath page 16, line 19. You said, "I asked the Prosecutor to refresh my memory" and I put it to you that that happened 3rd through the 6th or the 10th of February 1998 when someone from the Prosecutor's Office "refreshed your recollection -- your memory" by telling you that you had some meetings with Ljubisa Beara, that you had two meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What's the basis for that question? I would be interested to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The basis of the question, Your Honour is his statement under oath that he asked the prosecutor to refresh his memory and I'm going to show him the February 1998 statement when he first mentioned Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I don't think his previous statement was made in the context. I don't think that the statement that you're referring to here on page 16 was made in the context of the 1998 statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're tying the two together as if the 1998 statement was cooked by the -- by the investigator and eaten by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Let me ask you: Colonel Boering --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I see Mr. Nicholls on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, that was exactly my objection, Your Honour. At page 16, line 19, the witness is very clear about the period he's talking about. He said "before I came here," meaning now, not in 1998. There is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Very well, Judge. Let's put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In 1998 you came in you gave a statement to Richard Butler who worked for the Office of the Prosecutor at the time. You remember Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'd have to see his face. I do remember being there around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So do you have any independent recollection of spending four to five days or longer doing an interview with the Office of the Prosecutor, specifically Asif Syed and Richard Butler, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember it specifically with this man, but I was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And do you remember -- I don't care if you specifically remember the individual, but do you remember, sir, that it was the interviewers from the Office of the Prosecutor for this Tribunal who first mentioned to you Mr. Beara's name? You didn't mention it to them, they mentioned it to you. Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Could have been. Could be so, could be no, correct? I'll go on. You had weekly meetings with representatives from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because when you say, could be yes, could be not, is not a correct presentation of his answer. Your question was very specific. In other words, whether he was prompted by the Prosecution, by the investigator, and his answer was he does not remember that being the case. Which basically means no to your answer so it's not could be yes and could be no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the way I heard it and I read on the screen now, I heard it, "I don't remember." And when I hear "I don't remember" that means, well, I don't remember, could have been yes, could have been no. That's how I took it. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Colonel, let's be clear about this. Mr. Meek's question was a very simple one and he asked you that -- he suggested to you that it was the interviewers from the Office of the Prosecutor for this Tribunal who first mentioned to you Mr. Beara's name, and then he was very specific, he asked -- he told you, "You didn't mention it to them. They mentioned it to you. Do you remember that, sir?" And your answer was, "No, I don't remember that." What did you mean by your answer? That in other words it could have been the case or that it certainly wasn't the case that Beara's name was first mentioned to you by the Prosecutor? Or by the investigator, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Beara's name was definitely not the first one mentioned by the Prosecutor. Perhaps in an old DutchBat report this could be investigated, in one of the archives. I may have mentioned this internally to DutchBat after the first meetings with Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Make sure that this is not an interpretation problem. When I read your answer here in the transcript, "Colonel Beara's name was definitely not the first one mentioned by the Prosecutor," to me means that the Prosecutor mentioned a list of names on which Beara's was not the first one but basically it would still mean that the names were forthcoming from the investigator and not from yourself. Is that what you meant to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned the name. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it was a problem of interpretation, Mr. Meek. As I suspected it to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not going to really disagree with you but I don't believe it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The OTP mentioned names to you in that 1998 interview, did they not, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was about eight years ago, and of course I mentioned names of people I had seen and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I had hoped I wouldn't start the week like this but it seems I was hoping against hope. The question was not whether you mentioned, started mentioning names to the investigator but whether it's true that the investigators started mentioning names to you. Let's do it in a different manner. During this 1998 interview, did you mention names to the investigator which the investigator himself --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- had not mentioned to you before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: He didn't wait for the Dutch interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And did it also happen during that interview, 1998, that the investigator or investigators mentioned also to you names that you yourself had not mentioned to them until then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And there is where it ends as far as I'm concerned because the next was -- would have been, was Beara amongst them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, judge. I think that's as clear as mud but we'll go forward, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, you'll agree with me that the first time you mentioned Mr. Beara's name was approximately three years after the event, in 1998?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I presume, since you have testified previously in other cases in this Tribunal, that you also asked the Prosecutor in those cases to refresh your memory on events, did you not, like you did in this case?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know where you're going with these questions. They seem to repeat themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Colonel Boering, we are now talking about 2000, prior to your testifying in the Krstic case. Do you recall testifying in the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Will you agree with me, and the Trial Chamber can take judicial notice of his own files and that transcript, you never mentioned Mr. Beara in your entire testimony in that case. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. 2003, you testified in the Blagojevic and Jokic case. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Colonel Boering, do you remember that in your direct testimony, that means questions you answered from the Prosecutor, put to you in that case, you never mentioned Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber could take judicial notice of the direct examination in that case. Colonel Beara [sic], you don't ever remember them mentioning Mr. Beara in any of your previous testimony before this case; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this moment, I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you recall, in the spring of 1995, there being a helicopter crash in the vicinity of where you were stationed?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A helicopter did crash at one time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: For the record, do you recall approximately the month of that helicopter crash?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us who was riding in the helicopter when it crashed?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, presumably it had to do with Muslim ABiH, and if I remember correctly, there were some people who died and in the enclave people were buried, and people were secretive about it, as to who was -- were involved at the funeral service. But, yes, yes. Yes, there was a link, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did you ever determine or did DutchBat ever determine that the ABiH were bringing in weapons or ammunition when that helicopter went down?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that this was clear evidence. It was a suspicion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, it was approximately how long after that that you were at the Hotel Fontana and had a meeting with Major Nikolic and there were other officers from DutchBat and Mr. Beara was there? Do you recall? Was it several weeks or a month or --

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whether there was a link in the time, not really, but I suspect a couple of weeks afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you had weekly meetings with both the ABiH representatives and the Serbian representatives, correct, at the Fontana?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: ABiH was not -- I mean, the meeting was in Srebrenica and the Serbian representative was in Fontana. Serbian representative might have been once every two weeks at Yellow Bridge and in Fontana you could say once every two months perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And do you recall the meeting where you met Mr. Beara at the Fontana Hotel along with, besides yourself, was Major Rave and Piet Hein or one or the other?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can remember that there was this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: How many DutchBat or United Nations personnel were with you besides yourself and Sergeant-Major Rave or Piet Hein or both?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps a fourth person but I don't know exactly. It had to do with -- if Piet Hein was there, it had to do with trade in Fontana. Drinks and food was also purchased for DutchBat at Fontana so perhaps he also had a driver with him, you know, to load the truck with food and drink. We paid for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, do you recall there being two African Dutch soldiers or African United Nations soldiers with you on that day?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember, but -- on one or two occasions there would be -- the UNMO from Srebrenica would come along, could be but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And let me refresh your recollection, if I can. Do you recall that on that meeting, it was a luncheon meeting, and that you had food and you had drinks, you had meat, lamb, fish, you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, specifically, whether it was at that meeting, I do not know, but what I do remember is that when we went to pick up merchandise, often there was a lunch linked to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you recall that it was a luncheon-type meeting where you met Mr. Beara at the Fontana Hotel, sir?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you remember that there was a woman there?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you remember there were two black soldiers there that were going to sit at another table until Mr. Beara said no, come sit with us, and you put a separate table at the end so that the black soldiers could sit with you and eat lunch? Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. You do remember, though, that Mr. Beara was very interested in who was in that helicopter when it went down. Do you remember that, sir, or not?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was in a conversation with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And before we go any further, after that meeting, at the Fontana Hotel, where you had the luncheon and had the drinks and lunch, et cetera, you never shared -- you never saw Mr. Beara again, nor did you ever share any information with him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the second meeting with Colonel Beara, if I'm correct, and after that I didn't see him any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, little bit before that meeting that you claim was the second meeting, do you recall a village named Vlasic which had been burned by the ABiH soldiers who had left on raids during the night, V-l-a-s-i-c-h [sic], Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at this point, I myself don't remember the village Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Let me try to refresh your recollection. This was an incident where seven Serbs were killed, they were seven woodcutters, and they had been killed and the houses burned by the ABiH soldiers coming out of the enclave? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You do remember, don't you, Colonel Boering, that the ABiH soldiers would frequently make raids on the outlying Serbian villages at night from the enclave, correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That occurred regularly. I myself did not see it, but I -- it was reported to me often.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you've indicated at least in your written report in 1998, three years after these events, that Mr. Beara was extremely interested in knowing the whereabouts of Naser Oric. Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And didn't he, in fact, ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Nicholls? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just want to be clear for the record, the question was asked about a written report in 1998. Is that the ICTY statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you both.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. Beara asked you, didn't he, various questions about Naser Oric, if he was in the helicopter, if you knew where he was, what exactly was his position with the ABiH army. Do you remember that, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you remember Mr. Beara telling you that it was untenable that the ABiH army was continually leaving the enclave on raids at night and burning Serbian villages and killing Serb civilians and raping the women and that if he could meet with him and try to talk some sense into him maybe these raids would stop?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember something like that, that Colonel Beara indicated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And do you recall that Mr. Beara informed you, Colonel Boering, that the Serbian population in that vicinity was putting a lot of pressure on the VRS to stop these nightly raids and that the army was getting a lot of pressure? Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, you've testified that it was your knowledge that this was happening. You can understand how the VRS army may have been getting a lot of pressure because of these raids and this killing and plundering, correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because we need to clarify this, especially after your last question. On page 27, lines 13 to 17, you were asked a question, the following question by Mr. Meek: "You do remember, don't you, Colonel Boering, that the ABiH soldiers would frequently make raids on the outlying Serbian villages at night from the enclave, correct?" And you answered, according to the transcript, "Yes, that occurred regularly. I myself did not see it but it was reported to me often." If you could, please explain to us who used to report this to you and how often you would receive such reports? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the information we received of these events mainly came from the side of VRS, Major Nikolic, Momir Nikolic, and did not come from the ABiH side itself. So it was unilateral information that we could not check and we didn't have any liberty or freedom of action outside the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And how often?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You could say if there was a meeting with Major Momir Nikolic once every two, sometimes three weeks, this would be one of the standard subjects that he would talk about. And sometimes he actually also indicated the location and the nature of the event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Colonel Boering, just to follow up on that, there would be nothing abnormal about you having those reports from, for example, Major Nikolic, rather than an ABiH contact coming in and telling you and bragging to you about how they had just burned down a Serbian village last night and killed seven people, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need to go into this. It's so obvious, Mr. Meek. The whole purpose of the question was to elicit information from the witness whether the DutchBat could investigate or keep itself informed from independent sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Colonel Boering, I want to ask you one question real briefly. One of your missions was to demilitarise the enclave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And you would agree with me that if you would have done your job, that the ABiH army would not have been leaving on these night-time raids, correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't have the mandate to search houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you're familiar with your colleague, Eelco Koster, a DutchBat soldier, correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I would like to read you about two sentences from a statement he made to the Office of the Prosecutor on 25 and 26 September 1995. I will put it on in English, Judge, I do not have B/C/S. It is Exhibit number D -- 2 D00010.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just, Your Honour, I thought you made a ruling on this the other day that we would be putting statements to the witnesses without pitting witnesses against one another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is he a witness? Does he -- does this Mr. Koster or Officer Koster, give evidence in this Tribunal or not? Because from the way Mr. Meek put it, he's going to show us a statement that he made, an out-of-court statement and not testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That makes a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It's on page 6 of the English version, third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because I think we have a problem. I am not seeing -- did you hand it over to the staff for incorporation in the e-court system?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I believe it was scanned to e-court. I have a clean copy if you just want to put the front page and page 6. It will only take a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's resort to that. In the meantime, someone checks, please. It's not? I'm informed that it's not, Mr. Meek. It's not amongst the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'll check with Ms. Mulder, Your Honour. It should have been. For the record I just want to show him the very first page showing that it's soldier Koster making this statement, 25, 26 September, 1995 and then go to page 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. One moment. Because contrary to what I have been informed it can be -- it is there. It is there, 2 D? That's the reference, Judge Kwon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 2 D00010. I have even the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We found it. It exists, there is also the relative or corresponding translation. Thank you, Judge Kwon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And Colonel, please just look at the third paragraph down, if you'll just review that briefly, starts with, "until mid-June, I turned out three or four times with my unit from the compound in the direction of Srebrenica."

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: We need page 6 on the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Page 6, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Could zoom in on the third paragraph once we get there. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, have you had a chance just to review that third paragraph? It's not long.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you agree with your colleague Koster, when he stated because he was out in the enclave, "it struck me that each time we turned out, there were more Muslim fighters in the town than before. At that time we were no longer able to fulfil the policy requirements of the demilitarised zone. By this I mean that there were so many Muslim fighters walking around armed that we UN soldiers were incapable of disarming these people." Do you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself didn't see it the way he refers to it. I mean it's his statement. But in due course, it became more difficult to disarm ABiH. That was a problem for the whole of DutchBat. I know about that. But this incident, this report, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. And again, according to your colleague Koster's statement, this was by mid-June, a month before the fall, there were so many armed Muslim fighters that they couldn't disarm them. And you'll agree with me that Koster was out and about more than you were?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So you don't dispute that DutchBat just couldn't disarm the Muslims from June on?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that from mid-June, they sort of turned a blind eye and allowed for it, if Muslim fighters, armed Muslim fighters walked around with Kalashnikovs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just a clarification. Line 12, well, "I think that from mid-June, they sort of turned a blind eye." "They" who? Who are you referring to? Who turned a blind eye?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DutchBat itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I want to talk briefly with you about your alleged meeting, first meeting, with Mr. Beara. When was that again, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, and that brings us back to my notes. That was somewhere in March, end of March, early April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Who called that meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to my recollection, this person came from VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So it's your testimony that some person came from the VRS, personally, and asked you to come to a meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. For that we had Petar as an interpreter in Bratunac, and he would contact us by mobile phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: When I read your answer, that Petar as an interpreter would contact you by mobile phone, Colonel, I want to know do you have a specific recollection of who it was that contacted you about this purported meeting you Chamber you had with Mr. Beara and how was it done? Was it in person? Was it mobile phone? Was it fax? Please tell me.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take it that things went through Petar, through a sort of walkie-talkie connection. We did not have fax connections and sometimes we would get a message from Yellow Bridge to the post yellow papa, OP-Papa, that something had been seen but as to this meeting and how this meeting was requested, I do not know, not 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. That was my only question. You are really don't know how it came about. Now, what time, if you know, and if you don't know, please just say, "I don't know." What time were you advised that someone wanted you to come to the Jovo check-point?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the time, I'm not sure about that time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I only have about ten minutes left, Your Honour. Now would be a good time to take a break. I'll show the usher which short debriefing statements I have in English and -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Colonel Boering, I'm going to try to get through this very quickly. Over the break, you were given four different copies of documents from your Srebrenica debriefing by the Royal Netherlands Army, correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received four documents from you. If you look at them carefully see that there is a question mark on one. That's somebody else who's also named Boering. So the statement by soldier Boering is not my statement and I am familiar with the other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And for the record, you never mentioned Mr. Beara in any of those debriefings, did you?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's because of the purpose of this investigation. It was a brief investigation under the aegis of the military police focused on the role of DutchBat and possible crimes we might have seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Colonel Boering, please, maybe it's translation, I don't know, not to be rude, but I didn't ask you about the purpose of these debriefings. My simple question was: Mr. Beara was never mentioned, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained why he wasn't mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. Briefly back earlier, page 11, line 7, you testified that the battalion drafted a daily situation report to the superiors and sometimes there is a paragraph about CIMIC. And what exactly is CIMIC? It's misspelled in the record. It should be CIMIC, correct, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. CIMIC was -- in fact the role it was an unclear reference to the support for the local populace. CIMIC stands for civil military contacts. So partly civilian, if you're in touch with the local population; MI denotes military. So it's an explanation for military contacts with the civilians for carrying out projects.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, going back to this purported first meeting by Jovo check-point, we've already established you have no independent recollection of how you were invited to such a meeting. I'm going to ask you how many VRS soldiers met you in no-man's land when you said you were -- testified earlier that you were briefly kidnapped.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps about four men, two to four.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: How did you arrive at the beginning of the no-man's land that you are telling us you had to cross to get to check-point Jovo?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I drove there in the military Mercedes, and at OP-Papa, our observation post, I got out of the vehicle and walked from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Were you by yourself, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. A colleague was with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: What's that colleague's name?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Melchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You weren't really detained by these soldiers, were you?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was taken away under the threat of a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And where did these soldiers take you, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: To yellow bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's check-point Jovo, correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So would they have been some sort of escort? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, an armed escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: It was for your protection, do you believe?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him finish. I think there is a very straight way of dealing with it. Were you disarmed, Colonel, or were you allowed to carry our weapon with you throughout this entire operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was never disarmed in the entire period. I was carrying a pistol, but I don't use it as an elo [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That basically explains what meaning or what understanding we should have of being kidnapped, because that's -- any way, I think we can go straight to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: In your direct examination, Colonel, you were very vague about what transpired during that first meeting in regards what you and Mr. Beara purportedly spoke about. Could you clarify that, please?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the purpose of the meeting was to obtain information from the VRS about potential ABiH positions in the enclave and the conversation was clearly focused on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you remember specifically speaking to this individual who you claim was Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. An interpreter was present as well, so I was able to speak with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of this interpreter?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Petar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. What was it, then, that -- what was the subject more specifically of this conversation you purportedly had at check-point Jovo with Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe I already indicated that in my previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yeah. Your indication, Colonel in your previous answer was, "I think that the purpose of the meeting was to obtain information from the VRS about potential ABiH positions in the enclave." So my question is: You really don't know, do you? You just think, number 1, and number 2, I just asked you to be more specific. If you have no independent recollection today, just tell me and I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The questions were very focused from Colonel Beara as to what I knew about the ABiH troops in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So would it be a fair statement, he asked you that one question and the meeting was over?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you answer that question. It would also mean that what we have as his answer in lines 22 to 24 on the previous page is the exactly the opposite of what he meant or what he was supposedly would have stated and I think that's again a problem of interpretation. Because if you read those three lines, basically means that the purpose of the meeting -- meeting originates from him and not from the VRS or from Beara. And the purpose precisely was to obtain information about potential ABiH position from the VRS themselves which I don't think is exactly -- is -- reflects what the witness says. Or said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Colonel, you did actually answer that it was the VRS wanting information, but be that as it may, let me ask this question: Do you recall today specifically any individuals within the ABiH army in the enclave that Mr. Beara would have asked you about at that purported meeting?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was interested in Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: How about the ABiH commander Zulfo? Do you recall that or not?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: He probably did that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: How did you get back to the base from that meeting? Did you have a flashlight? Did the VRS soldiers take you back to your Mercedes Benz, or do you recall?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that any more. I did return to the base.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. How long did the meeting take, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps 15 minutes or 30 minutes, no longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Earlier on in your testimony in regards to reports, I think you indicated that you kept a personal diary. Did I hear you correctly, sir?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I kept notes of various meetings, but it wasn't a real diary that I kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you have any of those notes today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What's the objection, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you another question. Where are those notes, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: My notes, I don't have any notes at home. All I have are a few statements, most of them aren't at home either. And I threw most of them out, or it didn't arrive from the enclave back at my home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Your last answer is going to draw another question. You say, "I threw most of them out or it didn't arrive." Are you telling me, sir, that you have some of the notes but not all of them? Or not most of them?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, very briefly, earlier on this morning you testified that you were made aware of the ABiH soldiers leaving the compound during the nights and raiding nearby Serbian villages. My question, sir, is: Didn't the United Nations have other soldiers outside the enclave and did you ever make any inquiries to them to verify that, in fact, this was happening?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't personally involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you tell me who at DutchBat III would have been involved in that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps Colonel Karremans himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And speaking of Colonel Karremans, I believe you and Colonel Karremans drove together to the Hotel Fontana on the 11th of July and drove back from that first meeting, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended the meeting with him. But whether we drove there together, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, sir, you never met or saw Mr. Beara in July of 1995, did you?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't consciously meet him. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You never saw him at the Hotel Fontana during any of those meetings where Mladic was present, did you?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You never saw him anywhere in Bratunac, did you?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we talking about July now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Then I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You never saw him anywhere in Srebrenica, did you, sir? July 1995.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You never saw Mr. Beara anywhere in Potocari, did you, sir, in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see him anywhere in July 1995 so we could go on for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, he's telling you, you could continue mentioning about another two dozen places and his answer is going to always be the same, in July I never saw him anywhere. Was that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify with this witness that he never saw Mr. Beara again after the Hotel Fontana meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That was my objection that he said, I didn't see him in July 1995, so he could have run through a hundred --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And Mr. Ostojic wants me to ask this question which I'm sure will draw an objection: You never saw Mr. Beara, did you, when you took the column of refugees out on the 12th of July? Did you?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, sir, my only last -- my last question is: In all of your testimony you've stated that your memory has faded, it's worse than now it was in 1995, it was worse in 1998 than it was in 1995. Can you explain to me and explain to this Trial Chamber how it is that your memory seems to get better whether it comes to Mr. Beara when it seems to be worse when it comes to everybody else and every other situation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Objection. One, it's a complete mischaracterisation of what he said. He never testified that his memory about Beara was worse in 1998 than it was in 1995. And second, this -- objection is argumentative, how do you explain that your memory is getting better now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Colonel, we have full trust in your ability to answer this question. Go ahead and answer the question, please. Whichever way you like. It's being suggested to you, I will repeat the question. It's being suggested to you that on the basis -- apart or in spite of the fact that you said that as time goes by your memory fades, and it's worse now than it was in 1995, if you want to comment on that, can you explain to the Trial Chamber how it is, according to Mr. Meek, that your memory seems to get better when you're dealing with questions relating to Mr. Beara and while it seems to get worse, that's your memory, when you're dealing with questions touching on everyone else and every other situation. So it's divided into various parts and small sections. I trust you can answer the question. If you need assistance from the Trial Chamber, we'll give you assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the different preliminary investigations by the Prosecutor, and the various testimony hearings by the Tribunal and other institutions, I was obviously asked repeatedly about the incidents and what I saw. If you consider -- if you look at the first statement that was quickly -- which was made soon afterwards and which I read during the break, that was a very brief, focused investigation in which several individuals did not come up. Later on, various investigations were conducted relatively quickly. Some were into depth. Others went into greater depth about certain incidents in which links were established. This obviously relates to sorting out the roles of individuals in the Srebrenica investigation, and that brings up people on photographs and happenings, and the questions become more in depth, and I'm firmly convinced that this holds true for Colonel Beara as well, that I met him and that it has always stuck in my memory is clear to me personally. It's just that at the moment it was asked and elaborated on, that was a bit later. And personally, I was not forced to look at something and say that this is him. That wasn't the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you are answering the question, Colonel. Let me help you a little bit and we try to conclude the cross-examination here, unless Mr. Meek has got more questions. It's being put to you that you remember much more about Colonel Beara than about anyone else. Do you accept that proposition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's also being put to you that while you are forgetful about several events and about several people, you're not forgetful at all about Mr. Beara or Colonel Beara. Do you accept that proposition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do you mean by "yes"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember meeting him twice and those incidents were described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's a question of interpretation again. The proposition is that you remember more about Mr. Beara than about anything else, about other people and other circumstances where you tend to forget. This is what is being put to you. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That's not an acceptable proposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. It's back to you, Mr. Meek, if you wants could conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I do, Judge. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
