utterances.text: Colonel Boering, in your long answer up here, you mentioned documents you looked at on the break, correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And the documents you looked at on the break were given prior to 1998 but after July of 1995, correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are statements of September, October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Then in September 1995, and you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, we've talked about it this morning, you did not take that statement back with you in the break room, did you?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was taken from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you looked at that this morning and I named off probably four to five contacts you made in the ABiH army and in the VRS army, didn't I, sir?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And none of those contacts, none of those important or people you thought were important were Mr. Beara, were they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer that question, Colonel. You've put this question several times already. He's given you a straight answer already. Mr. Meek, please, your next question, which should not be a repetition of what you have asked already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You've testified on direct examination that at this purported first meeting, you were ambushed, you were kidnapped, you were taken hostage. Did you report that to anybody?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I told Mr. Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So perhaps Colonel Karremans would have some independent recollection or a report on that. Is that what your testimony is, sir? If you know.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you'd have to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. And in your answer to Judge Agius's question earlier, you said that, "I met him," being Colonel Beara and it's always stuck in my memory, it's clear to me personally. Then you said, "it's just that at the moment it was asked and elaborated on, that was a bit later." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, my question to you, Colonel, is: That part of your answer relates to the moment that the OTP investigators asked you about Mr. Beara and elaborated on Mr. Beara, and that's when you remembered everything, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What's your objection, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just that this ground has been gone over. He's been asked and answered, and Mr. Meek has no basis for putting that as a fact whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We are divided on this but I'll repeat the question to you and please answer it and that will be the last time we are touching on this. The question Mr. Meek asked you, Colonel, is the following: "Referring to a previous deposition on your part, he said that part of your answer relates to the moment that the OTP investigators asked you about Mr. Beara and elaborated on Mr. Beara and that's when you remembered everything; isn't that true?" What's your answer? In other words, it's being put to you that your memory of Mr. Beara and your meetings with him came back to you when you were specifically asked about Mr. Beara. But what -- where you would answer -- you need to answer that question and also, of course -- answer that question, first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It was not mentioned after the Prosecutor came up with it first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I think this is precisely why we have to stop on this. The witness has already answered this question in -- several times in whichever form it was put to you. He's making it very clear to you, Mr. Meek, that the mentioning of Mr. Beara originated from him and not from the Prosecutor. He's answered that question several times and I think you've tried again and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: All right. Then I will only ask one other question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And that wasn't until 1998, three years after the incident, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A question you've asked and he's answered it already before. So you don't need to answer it, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Meek. Now, what's the problem, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No problem, I was just wondering if we could get an estimate of how much time remains. We do have a witness available today. I take it we are not probably going to reach him but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I don't see why we should have had a witness -- another witness available today when I made it clear last time based on the estimates that I had that Colonel will be testifying the entire day of today and probably, being a conservative estimate, the entire day of tomorrow or most of it. In fact I told him so on Friday before he left. Yes, Madam Nikolic, who is representing Drago Nikolic here will be cross-examining you. You had estimated 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel Boering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you proceed, Mr. Lazarevic, I noticed you've taken on board new company unannounced. What's that about?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise for this, Your Honour. Perhaps I should have announced Mr. Dragomir Djukic's presence here. This is our case manager instead of Mr. Tatjana Cmeric, who will be absent during this week, and he's not wearing a robe because he's not a lawyer and that's the reason why he's not wearing a robe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you for that information. Madam Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Colonel Boering, on your direct and on your cross-examination, you were shown a document. That's why I would like the witness to be shown a 65 ter document number 0531. This is a report, a fax, that your commander, Karremans, sent on the 12th of July to the commanders in Zagreb, Sarajevo, Tuzla, and the Hague. In that he reported on the meeting with Mladic on the 17th of July -- on the 11th of July. Can we please turn to page 2?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just a moment, because my system encountered a problem and I have lost everything. So go ahead. Go ahead. I will recover everything myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Under item 6, which you discussed with Mr. Nicholls, under A and B, you provided your opinion of the events. I'm going to read to you what your force commander under C wrote down. "To find suitable representatives among the civilians because the official authorities are for certain reasons not available." Under D: "To find representatives among the military authorities because they are trying to fight for a corridor to the Tuzla area and will not show up any way because of purely personal reasons. I cannot force ABiH troops to hand over their weapons." In your opinion, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As I was reading all your statements and your testimonies, at the beginning, owing to the intervention of the Presiding Judge, will you agree with me that all the time when you mentioned the name Nikolic you meant Momir Nikolic, the liaison officer with the DutchBat from the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You met with him almost every other week. You had a number of contacts. You exchanged information. Did you trust Major Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can point out one event, one -- yeah, event, to indicate how far trust can go. At a certain point I had to come to Yellow Bridge. A number of VRS soldiers saw me coming, and I issued a message, I was given a message and I needed to take some time to look through it, and I was told to leave in one or two minutes or they would have to shoot me. And I had the distinct impression that that was going to happen. So I assumed it was a man, a man word [as interpreted] Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Two things. Number 1, line 5 of page 50, I distinctly heard the witness saying that he issued a message. Number of VRS soldiers saw me coming and I issued a message. Was it you who issued a message?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And initially in the transcript, I saw the I appearing and then it disappeared. The other thing is the last three lines, I don't understand at least. They are confusing. So it says, "I issued a message I was given a message and I need to take some time to look through it and I was told to leave in one or two minutes or they would have to shoot me and I had the distinct impression that that was going to happen. So I assumed it was a man, a man, Mr. Nikolic." It's this last part. So I assumed it was a man, a man, Mr. Nikolic, that I would like you to explain because as it is in the transcript, it is not clear enough. Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried to describe, you know, that if he pointed out something, if he indicated something, if he did something, you could assume that that was what he meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think I have to take you back to the message then. You were given a message, you said. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was it in writing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A letter, I think, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And was it a signed letter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who was the signatory? Who had signed it? Whose signature --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is a letter that were you carrying with you which you handed to the VRS soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And did the VRS soldiers communicate any message to you in writing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They gave me the message that this has been received, this message, and we will not be contacting you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And there message that they gave you, not the one that you gave them, the one that they gave you, was it a written message? And if it was, was it signed? And by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the latter, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you seem to me to put the blame for all this that happened on that particular occasion on Momir Nikolic. Why do you do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The question was whether I trusted Major Nikolic. And my answer is yes, I trust him. He does what he says. So it's not that he's untrustworthy. This was just an example, and I assumed he's very trustworthy, so trustworthy that I've got to be careful and I've got to get away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, you're telling us that if the message that you got back was, go back because we'll shoot you, that they would be true to their words, including Momir Nikolic and indeed if you tried not to go back you would indeed be shot? Is that what you meant to convey to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was threatened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think it's clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Madam Nikolic. Mr. Lazarevic? Or yes? You're now going to be cross-examined on behalf of Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. How long do you think you'll be cross-examining this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't received interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We believe that we will do our cross-examination within the scope of one hour. It will take us an hour, as we planned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, based on your testimony so far, I understand that from January 1995, until you left the enclave, you worked as a liaison officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During that period of time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I haven't heard an answer from the witness and I don't want to hear it because he's been asked this question and answered it several times. So let's move to the basics of your cross-examination, Mr. Stojanovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During this period of time you met up with the representatives of the VRS and with the representatives of the civilian and military authorities in the enclave of Srebrenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You had a number of contacts with Ramiz Becirevic, who represented BiH army and Momir Nikolic who represented the army of Republika Srpska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Momir Nikolic represented the Bratunac Brigade at first, and reports regularly we were -- we were regularly able to send messages to other brigades through him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I also understand that you met Nesib Mandzic on several occasions before you proposed his name as the representative of refugees from Potocari and this happened at your meeting with General Mladic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please help us and comment upon a video clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For identification, Your Honours, the number is ERN number is V 0004458. This is Exhibit P01557, and this is a video clip starting from 7.42 to 9.10 seconds. Can we please be shown this video clip?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, we still don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We seem to have a technical problem. If the technicians could help us. I apologise to you, Mr. Stojanovic. I can't help you beyond apologising. Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We may be able to play it if, perhaps, I don't know if counsel wants to walk around, make sure we are on exactly the same page of the clip. I think we are. Or we can play it ourselves. I think we've got the numbers right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we do that, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So if I got Mr. Stojanovic correct before, he wants to shows us from 7.42 to 9.10. So that's just under two minutes of --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I believe that we can overcome this obstacle and I will kindly ask Ms. Janet to help us with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, this is the event --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's see it first and then you explain to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now your question and explain to the witness whatever you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, can you recognise the man on this still?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose you mean the man wearing a light blue jacket with his hands extended towards -- outward, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recognise him. This is the first time I'm seeing this recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are at still 7.48.5. Yes. Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please continue playing the video and then I will ask you again to stop at one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, do you recognise the person in the middle of this still wearing a military uniform sporting a mustache and maybe a beard as well?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's Ramiz Becerovic, if I'm right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's try and see if you can help us and tell us whether the first person on the first still could have been Nesib Mandzic or not.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recognise him on that recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can you just bear with me? I would like to advise the Trial Chamber that we stopped the video clip at 8.39 minutes and that the witness recognised Ramiz Becerovic on that still.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that you had several meetings with Mr. Mandzic and could you please tell us what you discussed during those meetings, what the topic of your conversations was.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were exclusively about school-related matters. We are talking about the meetings prior to his selection as representative of the population. Up to that point, my only dealings with him were when I visited his school and we didn't talk about anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you personally think that Mr. Mandzic would be a good representative, and why did you put his name forward at this meeting in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to know before that whether it was he who put the name of Mr. Mandzic or whether it was Mr. Karremans. Or he and Mr. Karremans together.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, were you the one who proposed Mr. Mandzic as the representative at the meeting in the Fontana Hotel?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My next question is relative to the one that I asked you just a minute ago. Why did you decide to do that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, when I drove back from Srebrenica to Potocari, we, the Sergeant-Major Rave and I, opened some gates so that the refugees would have some room, and I think in the corner of my eye I noticed Nesib Mandzic. That's how it sticks in my memory and that's how I thought, gee, we need somebody, I saw somebody, can we find him? It's in my memory about like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember whether Mr. Mandzic had any previous political engagements?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't notice that; not in his actions and not in the course of the conversations I had with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that in that period of April, May, and June of 1995, that there were some political conflicts within the enclave of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I certainly know that because there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there people in power as well as their opposition?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Opposition existed there, and there was a struggle between the opposition and the potentates. I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps you can assist us in the following: Can you tell us who do you have in mind when you say people in power?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: What comes to mind? I don't remember any names, but what comes to mind is that one of the persons in the opposition had formed an opposition party and requested DutchBat for protection because they felt threatened. I remember discussing that with Sergeant-Major Rave, that we did not provide such protection, and that we regarded this as an internal issue within the enclave. I remember that the next day, at least one of those opposition members was seriously injured and the leadership of the enclave in our weekly meeting urged us not to seek any contacts without their involvement. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who do you believe were the potentates in the enclave, the power-wielders?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The potentates in the enclave, there was one part, it was Zulfo in the west, at the rear it was Tursunovic or something like that, and in the rest of the area it was Naser Oric with a group, and he was in charge of that group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Talking of April, May, and June of 1995. It's my understanding from what I have heard in this case that Naser Oric was air-lifted to Tuzla in April. So what about the rest of April, May, and June of 1995? He wasn't there supposedly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then he wasn't there, and then we would deal with the person you would see in the centre of that image, but there certainly was contact with Naser Oric. My impression was those were the instructions. So you don't have to be in charge to be present [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, we heard the name of Momir Nikolic mentioned often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry I just think there might be an error in the transcript. I want to make sure. I think it says you don't have to be in charge to be present. I think it must be the other way around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I take it. I think that we do have a slight problem of interpretation this morning so basically I agree with you. Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, what position did Mr. Momir Nikolic have at that time within the Bratunac Brigade, provided you know?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was our liaison. His actual role within the brigade was unclear, and he liked to keep it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he have any military rank?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We addressed him as Major Nikolic. That's how he was introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he also have the ranks on his shoulder?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Generally, the VRS did not have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Momir Nikolic ever tell you that he held the rank of major?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you contesting Momir Nikolic's rank, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Perhaps this is a good opportunity for me to try and prove at a later stage that indeed he did not have that rank. I'm trying to gain some information through this witness as regards that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then go ahead, because this could be -- this could be the only reason I could think of why you are putting these questions. So the question, Colonel, the question to you is, did Mr. Nikolic ever tell you that he held the rank of major?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I remember that he didn't want to address -- he didn't want to be addressed by his rank or his position. There was even an incident where he was addressed as commander of the Bratunac Brigade and he became so angry that he refused to deal with us for a while, so he [as interpreted] tried not to bring up his rank or his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who introduced him to you as Major Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that was General Zivanovic in early January. And also via my predecessors of DutchBat II, who preceded me and gave us a list of the people they were in touch with and their names and ranks. So based on that, it was Major Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During your examination-in-chief, you identified someone by the name of Colonel Jankovic as well. Can you assist us in telling us what his role was during those meetings at Hotel Fontana? How did you see him?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: His role was first of all to provide Mladic with direct assistance. That was why at one of the meetings he was seated directly next to him and occasionally he consulted with him. At the start of the first meeting, he was also Mladic's spokes person to Karremans, to convey messages correctly, and later on, you see in the video that Petar takes over that role. At the third video, I believe that Colonel Jankovic is seated in the background across from General Mladic taking notes. Later on, I wasn't involved, Colonel Jankovic was assigned to wrap matters up on site on behalf of General Mladic but I learned that through indirect observation, as a type of liaison from General Mladic to DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At those three meetings, did he raise any points? Did he engage in discussions?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. More -- his role was more to observe and to take notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that from hearsay or from other sources, you concluded that he were to wrap up things on the spot on behalf of General Mladic. Would you agree with me if I said that he was a sort of an executive who was tasked with carrying out Mladic's plans? Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be more inclined to say that he was the liaison toward DutchBat, to arrange things with DutchBat. So limited execution of General Mladic's plans, focused primarily on DutchBat. But that's not based on my personal observations. This is based on hindsight and hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say, "To carry out or implement Mladic's plans," what plans exactly do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the transport of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you hear for the first time of the separation of the able-bodied men from the rest?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could be during the first or the second meeting with General Mladic. At any rate, I certainly heard about it by the third meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I would kindly ask to you comment on a document and I would kindly ask the registrar to help us. This is our Exhibit 4 D15. We received this with the general collection forwarded via the EDS. The ERN number is 4 D000176 through 4 D000189. Unfortunately, Your Honours, up until this moment we haven't received the translation and I just wanted to read out the title and what follows is a list of names and hence I do not expect any problems. Colonel, sir, the title reads, "The list of war criminals known to the command of the 1st Light Infantry Bratunac Brigade who had committed war crimes in the areas of municipalities of Bratunac, Srebrenica, Milici, Vlasenica, and Skelani, and for whom there are indications that they are in Srebrenica." What follows is the various categories within the documents. First we have organisers and officials, then the command, and immediate perpetrators. The total number of people on the list is 387, and the date is the 12th of July 1995. My question relating to this document is the following: Do you know anything about this document? Is anything familiar?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this is the first time I'm seeing this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Momir Nikolic at any point mention this document to you in any way?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that, but I do remember that there were criminals, but as to whether he issued a list, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Since you mentioned there were criminals, what did that entail?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: By criminals, I mean the way Mr. Nikolic said it, war criminals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's get this clear because again I need to clarify this. What we have in the transcript is, "I do remember that there were criminals." What you meant to say, and correct me if I'm wrong, is that although you never saw such a list, Mr. Momir Nikolic did mention to you the existence of war criminals. Is that what you meant to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, you didn't mean to tell us that you had personal knowledge of the existence of war criminals amongst the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. There were reports of possible misconduct on the part of ABiH troops in the enclave, that might have perpetrated war crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I think that's clear enough. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, based on what you said today, and having in mind your statement given to the OTP on the 10th of February 1998, and for identification purposes this is at page 8, paragraph 2, where you mention the meeting of the 12th of July 1995 and the evacuation of the population. There you mention a meeting where Mladic spoke, and this was a meeting with General Smith, and you stated there as well that Mr. -- that Lieutenant Colonel Karremans was not to worry about that. Do you remember that part of your statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, if he's going to be asked questions on this event, then he needs to see the statement. So let's make it available to him, please, and we need to see it too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the registrar for assistance. This is a Defence Exhibit, the number being 4 D25, page 8, in the English, the second paragraph. Page 9 of the English, second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I believe you will be able to see that part of your statement on the screen before you, page 9, paragraph 2. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the paragraph with outlined, et cetera, Mladic outlined, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. The fourth line in particular is the portion that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but this does not reflect what we had in the transcript, again once more, in page 63, lines 16, 17, to 21, was -- according to the transcript, it was put to the witness as follows: He's being referred to this particular paragraph except that it is on page 8, according to the transcript and now we see that it is page 9, and he's told, where you mentioned the meeting of the 12th of July 1995 and the evacuation of the population, there you mention a meeting where Mladic spoke and this was a meeting with General Smith and you stated there as well that, something missing, that Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans was not to worry about that. It's exactly the opposite of what the relevant part of his statement describes, relevant part of the statement describes that first, Karremans objected to this but Mladic ignored his objection, and then Mladic retorted that General -- that he had met General Smith and Karremans should not bother about it. So your question now. I repeated all this to make the things clearer, not to anticipate your question, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, my question is the following: Who is General Smith?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Smith was the superior -- the level above us. He was not in Tuzla. I believe he was in Sarajevo. At any rate, he was the higher level. He could have been in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that on that occasion, General Mladic mentioned to Lieutenant Colonel Karremans that he had met with General Smith and that Lieutenant Colonel Karremans shouldn't worry about the issues raised?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what the statement says. So your question should be whether he confirms what is contained in the second paragraph, not the other way around or the way you put it. Colonel, from your own knowledge, do you confirm the contents of the second paragraph in this statement on page 9 or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at this time, that's not in my memory, but if I made such a statement at the time, then I assume that that was indeed the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I believe this would be a convenient moment nor our next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perfect. Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic and Mr. Nicholls. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. I see you standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, I stood before I rose -- it was the break. I just wanted to be clear for the transcript, the question was about issues raised but it's clear from the statement that it wasn't about issues, plural, but that Karremans objected to the separation of men for interrogation and that's what General Mladic said he should not worry about, not a range of issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The witness was referred only to the second paragraph on page 9, and the question that we have here, is it correct that on that occasion, General Mladic mentioned to Lieutenant Colonel Karremans that he had met with General Smith and that Lieutenant Colonel Karremans shouldn't worry about the issues raised. Whichever the issues were. This is the whole point that is put to the witness and in paragraph 2 we have precisely that. Mladic outlined evacuation plan for the refugees, Mladic agreed, et cetera, the men would be separated further, Karremans objected to this, but Mladic ignored him, Mladic said that he had met General Smith and said Karremans should not bother about it. The gist of the question put by Mr. Stojanovic is in relation to the fourth and fifth line and he actually repeated that he was referring to the fourth and fifth line. Correct me if I'm wrong, Mr. Stojanovic. But I don't think I am wrong. You were not discussing the issues, at least for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to inform the Court, I apologise, I won't be able to be here tomorrow. So Mr. McCloskey will handle any redirect, if there is any. I'm very sorry about that. It's something that has been scheduled for a long time and originally anticipated it would work with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls, for informing us. Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, after the third meeting at the Fontana on the 12th of July, you went to Potocari and after a short meeting with Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans and Major Franken, you returned to Bratunac again; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And there you met with Mr. Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And he told you to go back to Potocari because the evacuation was just about to start; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or that it had started already.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The meeting with Momir Nikolic, was that a spontaneous meeting or did you ask to see Mr. Nikolic again?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a spontaneous meeting. I drove there myself, without having an appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: However, at that moment, Mr. Momir Nikolic knew that the evacuation was just about to start or that it had just started; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us how you saw the role of Mr. Momir Nikolic in the evacuation and the separation of able-bodied men from the rest of the group?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself did not see him being present at Potocari, Mr. Nikolic, nor did I see him in the separation of the men. So I didn't actually see him being involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to ask to be shown Exhibit number 4 D16. This is a statement on the facts and the acceptance of guilt that Mr. Momir Nikolic provided. The ERN number of this document in the English version is 4 D000190 to 4 D000198. I would like to draw your attention to item 5 of this statement on facts and the acceptance of guilt provided by Momir Nikolic. Can you please focus on item 5? This is actually Momir Nikolic's guilty plea statement. It says here, after speaking to Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic and Kosovic [as interpreted], Colonel Jankovic left the Hotel Fontana and told me to coordinate the transportation of all the women and children and the separation of the able-bodied Muslim men.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see that, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Since we are not military personnel, could you please tell us, in your doctrine, what is understood by the term "coordination"? And I'm talking about the military terminology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honour, I have not such text in my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On one screen I have the English text and the corresponding text, translation into B/C/S. So I suppose if you press on e-court, the e-court button, you should have it. If you don't, let me know. E-court button. E-court. Do the rest have it? Yeah, I see you, Mr. Lazarevic, saying, for example that he can see it. Perhaps someone can help Mr. Zivanovic and we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Zivanovic should look at his monitor in between himself and Ms. Condon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. Let's proceed. Yes. I apologise to you, Mr. Stojanovic. So, Colonel, you were asked to explain to us the military significance of the term "to coordinate," "coordination," I take it in relation to an operation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're responsible for coordination, you will bring together the different parties and you will try to fine-tune the parties' interests so that the things happen as correctly as possible, as quickly as possible, and from your superior you can be given a coordinating authority so that you can act on behalf of a superior in rank. So in this case, I would think it's some sort of coordinator, as he himself indicates, for transport and separation, and that he received the authority from Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Just one more thing. This coordination, does it also imply the possibility of command over the units that are supposed to be coordinated amongst themselves, in keeping with the instructions that he received?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't go that far.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please go to item 6 of this statement, the last sentence thereof. In English, it is on page 3. Here, Mr. Momir Nikolic continues, and speaks about the facts and the acceptance of guilt and he says that in coordination with these units, that he mentioned previously, he coordinated and oversaw the transportation of the women and children to Kladanj and the separation and detention of the able-bodied Muslim men. Colonel, sir, do you still believe that the term "coordination" implies something that can be carried out without giving any orders or conveying any orders to the units which are being coordinated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just that's not exactly what the witness's answer was before so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I was toying with the idea of intervening myself because previously, he -- what the witness said, that he wouldn't go that far in agreeing with you because your question said, does it also imply the possibility of command over the units? So I take his answer meaning overall command. And he's saying it wouldn't go that far. But I didn't understand his answer to mean that it would exclude even the slightest measure of command. So perhaps you can direct him to that. Perhaps he can explain his previous answer. Because that's how I understood. Colonel, does your definition or understanding of "coordination" as previously conveyed to us means that you are excluding completely the possibility of even the slightest measure of command in the course of coordinating the operation or giving orders, in other words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's his answer, Mr. Stojanovic, and that's precisely how I understood it in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That was my understanding too, and I don't believe we need to dwell on this any further. This answer should suffice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, let us continue with the 12th of July. At around 1.30 p.m., after you had that contact with Mr. Nikolic, you returned again to Potocari. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You had to cross the yellow bridge and you had to pass by your observation post, is that so?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At the observation post, did you stop by and talk to some soldiers of the DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but it could be. Especially if you see some of your own soldiers, you would stop and you would ask, well, what's going on and how are you guys?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is only logical. Can you assist us and tell us, what name did you use for that observation post?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. OP-Papa, observation post papa.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, at around 1.30 p.m. On the 12th of July, members of the Dutch Battalion were still at that observation post; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know any more. Could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Upon your arrival in Potocari, you saw a large number of refugees boarding buses. I wanted to ask you this: The boarding of the buses, did it take place in only one particular spot or were people boarding several buses and trucks at the same time, as far as you could see?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were entering various buses and vehicles at once.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So there wasn't only a single place where the boarding was carried out but, rather, it encompassed an area?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The buses were lined up one behind the other, and they were stationary, and they were being loaded to capacity. So people were entering the bus at various places, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it directly in front of the UN base, or maybe to the left- or to the right-hand side of the UN base, looking towards the asphalt road?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the transportation was on the right-hand side of the road, around and near the base.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Among the group of refugees, did you see any members and fighters of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that you could recognise?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, could we please have your comment on a document? And I would kindly ask the registrar's assistance. This is 4 D17. The ERN being 4 D000208 through 4 D000209. Could we focus on the first page of this report? Unfortunately, Your Honours, we still haven't received a translation. But I will put only one sentence to the witness and I'm about to read it outloud. Colonel, sir, this is a document from the General Staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina dated the 12th of July 1995, as you can see in the upper left corner, issued at 1325, which is precisely the time where you were supposed to be in Potocari. Enver Hadzihasanovic, the Chief of the General Staff, addressed this to the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina via the 1st Corps command of the ABiH. It states the following: "Last night, around 2300 hours, we had 15.000 to 20.000 refugees who were seated in the area of combat activity, together with 300 fighters of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the camp in Potocari." Can you tell us approximately how many able-bodied men did you see in Potocari on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I walked through the group of refugees two or three times. It's difficult to estimate, but I certainly saw a few tens.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: A little while ago you identified the Chief of Staff of the 28th division as being Ramiz Becirevic. On the 11th of July, were you able to see him anywhere in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last time I saw him was in Srebrenica at the Bravo Company compound, when he requested safety for his wife, and I did not see him after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right to conclude that this was on the 10th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please assist us: A division comprises several brigades, is that so?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: A brigade comprises several battalions, is that so?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you were there as a Dutch Battalion, having the required manning strength, is that so?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the end, we were at about 60 per cent manning strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In order to conclude with this set of questions, I wanted to ask you this: On the 12th, you joined the first refugee convoy to Kladanj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was at the front of the convoy? Who headed it?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that I mentioned that a few times before, and identified these persons on photographs a few times as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You did, Colonel. I just wanted to create a foundation for my following questions. In terms of numbers, what -- where was your vehicle in the column?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very soon after we started driving, I tried to catch up with the column. I believe I was the second or the third vehicle. No buses were right in front of me. There was one passenger car with the individual concerned and perhaps another military vehicle but I don't remember that any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ask for your superior's permission to leave with that convoy or did you do that of your own accord?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was assigned to accompany them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who gave you that task, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Franken.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you have your personal weaponry with you?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My pistol and ten bullets. And as I mentioned earlier, that's -- you have that with you as a status symbol but it's not really for fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you mentioned that at a certain point in Kladanj, you were captured by some members of the AB and H, was the handgun taken away from you?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it taken away immediately, in Kladanj, or sometime later, when you left the area?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, immediately before we arrived in Kladanj, we encountered, I believe, the front reconnaissance of the ABiH, and they were suspicious of what was happening. They stopped us, took our weapons away, and took us away, or rather, we walked away with them, to their headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The next day, you continued on towards Split; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I travelled via Tuzla. In the end, after some interruptions, I reached Split. It may have taken me another two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who were you given permission from for you not to have to return to Srebrenica but, rather, to go on towards Split, if you were given that permission by anyone? Perhaps this was of your own will.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a Dutch colonel, Colonel Branz [phoen] in Tuzla. I spoke with him there and discussed this subject matter with him and he knew what was happening. I certainly didn't go off on my own. That wouldn't work. You need transportation, and helicopter, I even travelled part of the way in a caterpillar vehicle. You can't do that of your own accord.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In order to conclude, Colonel, sir, I still have something that is unclear to me. During your examination-in-chief on the 22nd of September, on page 17, lines 14 through 17 of the transcript, having been asked by the OTP how many men were separated and taken away in Tisce, in Luka, when you reached that area on the 12th of July, you responded, if you remember, "In my view, there were ten to 15 men, not more than that. There was great commotion and I couldn't move about freely." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember saying whether there was great consternation but I do remember saying that there were 10 to 15 men and that I did not have freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is precisely what I wanted to ask you. I would kindly ask the registrar to show us yet again Colonel Boering's statement of the 10th of February 1998, this being a Defence Exhibit, the number is 4 D25. In the English, this is page 11, paragraph 3. So page 11, paragraph 3. In the B/C/S, it is page 11, paragraph 1. Colonel, could you please focus on the middle part of the third paragraph? I wanted to read out one sentence only. "At one point, VRS soldiers separated two or three Muslims from the convoy. First they had to wait by the side of a vehicle and then they were taken a bit further on along the road. I don't know what happened to them." Colonel, I see a different number here, as regards the number of people who were separated from the rest of the convoy. The number here being two or three. Therefore, which option is correct?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that one needs to exclude the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I agree. You are right. Ten or 15 men always implies two or three. However, my question is simple: Were there two, three, 10 or 15 men that were separated?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the very first statement, you see, at a point that I state this is happening to two or three, it's possible that they were separated in other places as well but in my view, I certainly saw more being separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you say so to the Prosecutor's Office when you provided your statement in 1998, when your memory was much fresher, as you said yourself, than today, six years later? Or eight years later, rather.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will not insist on that. However, help me with this. The situation is very similar. It may be very important to us. Can the witness be shown the same document, page 10, paragraph 4, in the English version, please? The same statement, page 10, paragraph 4. In B/C/S, it is page 9, the penultimate paragraph on that page. The paragraph is very short and I'm going to read it to you in its entirety, Colonel. You say here, "When we returned to Potocari from Bratunac, I saw that Mladic was already there. The screening process had already started. The separation of Muslim males had begun. VRS soldiers were not inside the compound but they tried to enter. The separated men were taken to an unfinished house. I tried to go there, but I was stopped by the VRS soldiers." On your direct, you said as follows: "I entered that house." This is what you said. Help us with this. Did you or did you not enter the unfinished house, as you described it yourself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have to stop you, Mr. Stojanovic. This was -- question was dealt with, I don't know whether you were present here. I think you were not, in fact. But this question was put to the witness and he has answered it in no unclear terms. So I don't think he needs to be faced with it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this for the following reason. The way I understood you in response to my colleague from the Popovic team asked you why didn't you mention having seen passports in that house?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will the question continue or was the subject not supposed to be addressed? I'm a little bit unclear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic is seeking to attack your credibility, suggesting that you have no reason, plausible reason, why you never mentioned the passports before in your statement to anybody. This is -- and why I am allowing the question. But Mr. Stojanovic equally is obviously forgetting that we are three -- four professional judges here and not a lay jury. So we are not easily impressed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My last question to you is this: You saw the passports in the corner of that house. Why didn't you mention that in the statement that you provided to the Prosecutor's Office in 1998 and even before that, in 1995?

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to finish by asking the usher to put a document on the ELMO and I would kindly ask the witness, who has stated that he is familiar with the Cyrillic letter, to help us with this document and to try and read any of the three names of the towns which are indicated on this document. I have ample copies for the Trial Chamber and this will be my last question, Your Honours. This is the Cyrillic script and the names of the towns in Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, bearing in mind the fact that your knowledge of the Cyrillic script is limited, I would still ask you whether you can read the names of any of these three towns indicated on this piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: PIETER BOERING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can try the bottom one, Brecelija [phoen], something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the record, Your Honours, the towns mentioned here are in the vicinity of the place where the developments took place, and the names are Sekovici, Bijeljina, and Vlasenica. The bottom town is Vlasenica through which the column passed and the colonel tried to read the name of that third town. Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we adjourn, very quickly, Madam Fauveau, what's your anticipated time tomorrow?
